questions.story:
The Monkey’s Paw
Adapted from W. W. Jacobs

Passage 1
Without, the night was cold and wet, but in the small parlour of Laburnum Villa the blinds were drawn and the fire burned brightly. Father and son were at chess, the former possessing ideas about the game involving radical changes, putting his king into such sharp and unnecessary perils that it even provoked comment from the white-haired old lady knitting placidly by the fire.

Passage 2
Sergeant-Major Morris took the little paw from his pocket. “It had a spell put on it by an old fakir,” he said, “a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow. Three separate men could each have three wishes from it.” He held it out, and his manner was not encouraging.

Passage 3
“If you’ve had your three wishes, it’s no good to you now, Morris,” said the old man. “What did you do with it?” “I threw it on the fire,” replied the soldier. His face whitened as he said it, and the family exchanged a glance they did not explain. “Better let it burn,” he added abruptly, and when Mr White took it from the flames he said so again.

Passage 4
“I wish for two hundred pounds,” said the old man distinctly. A fine crash from the piano greeted the words, interrupted by a shuddering cry from the old man. His wife and son ran toward him. “It moved,” he cried, with a glance of disgust at the object as it lay on the floor. “As I wished, it twisted in my hand like a snake.”

Passage 5
The stranger stood at the gate a long while before he came in. He was well dressed, and he turned his hat in his hands, hesitating, before he spoke. “I was asked to call,” he said at last. “I come from Maw and Meggins.” The old lady started. “Is anything the matter? Has anything happened to Herbert? What is it?” Her husband interposed. “There, there, Mother,” he said hastily.

Passage 6
“He was caught in the machinery,” said the visitor in a low voice. There was no reply. The old woman’s face was white, her eyes staring, her breath inaudible. “The firm wishes me to convey their sincere sympathy with you in your great loss,” he continued, without looking round. “They admit no liability at all, but they wish to present you with a certain sum.” He gave the figure: two hundred pounds.
questions.question: Read Passage 5. What can be inferred about the stranger before he speaks?

options.text: He has come to deliver good news and is waiting for the right moment
He has lost his way and is unsure whether he has the correct house
He is bringing news he does not want to deliver
He is a friend of the family who has visited many times before

The stranger stood at the gate a long while before he came in. He was well dressed, and he turned his hat in his hands, hesitating, before he spoke. “I was asked to call,” he said at last. “I come from Maw and Meggins.” The old lady started. “Is anything the matter? Has anything happened to Herbert? What is it?” Her husband interposed. “There, there, Mother,” he said hastily.

Passage 6
“He was caught in the machinery,” said the visitor in a low voice. There was no reply. The poverty of working people in England at the time
The temptation to take what fate has not offered, and the price attached to it
The soldier’s memories of his years of service abroad

questions.story:
The Monkey’s Paw
Adapted from W. W. Jacobs

Passage 1
Without, the night was cold and wet, but in the small parlour of Laburnum Villa the blinds were drawn and the fire burned brightly. Father and son were at chess, the former possessing ideas about the game involving radical changes, putting his king into such sharp and unnecessary perils that it even provoked comment from the white-haired old lady knitting placidly by the fire.

Passage 2
Sergeant-Major Morris took the little paw from his pocket. “It had a spell put on it by an old fakir,” he said, “a very holy man. He wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow. Three separate men could each have three wishes from it.” He held it out, and his manner was not encouraging.

Passage 3
“If you’ve had your three wishes, it’s no good to you now, Morris,” said the old man. “What did you do with it?” “I threw it on the fire,” replied the soldier. His face whitened as he said it, and the family exchanged a glance they did not explain. “Better let it burn,” he added abruptly, and when Mr White took it from the flames he said so again.

Passage 4

His wife and son ran toward him. “It moved,” he cried, with a glance of disgust at the object as it lay on the floor. “As I wished, it twisted in my hand like a snake.”

questions.question:
Consider these two observations from the story:
Observation 1: Morris warns that those who interfere with fate do so to their sorrow, and twice urges that the paw be destroyed.
Observation 2: The exact sum wished for arrives, but only as compensation for a death.
Which statement best expresses the theme built from these observations?

options.text: Soldiers who travel abroad bring dangerous objects home with them
Factories should be made safer for the people who work in them
Families should not play games of chance in the evening
